claims.text: The starting material consists of W particles distributed within a Cu matrix.
The W particles have clean surfaces accessible to ALD precursors.
Low-temperature ALD can deposit a 20–30 nm conformal Cu or Cu-alloy coating on W particles below 300 °C.
The coated particles will be consolidated by HIP at 800–900 °C and 150–200 MPa for several hours in a reducing atmosphere.
Keeping ALD below 300 °C maintains coating conformality.
Precise control of HIP parameters will preserve the integrity of the ALD coating.
The process will produce a continuous, conformal Cu shell on each W particle.
The Cu shell will bridge the W–Cu interface.
The Cu shell will facilitate uniform wetting during HIP.
The Cu coating will promote intimate W–Cu contact and adhesion during HIP.
The Cu coating will fill interfacial gaps and minimize void formation.
A graded interfacial layer will alleviate W–Cu thermal-expansion mismatch under service conditions, including irradiation.
The ALD-plus-HIP process will provide near-perfect W–Cu interfacial bonding.
The ALD-plus-HIP composite will have significantly lower defect density than composites made by standard filling or melting techniques.
The ALD-plus-HIP composite will have superior thermal conductivity to composites made by standard filling or melting techniques.
The ALD-plus-HIP composite will have superior mechanical durability to composites made by standard filling or melting techniques.
Service temperatures must remain below an unspecified threshold at which interfacial integrity would be compromised.
The ALD-derived interface will retain improved thermal and mechanical performance after simulated irradiation.

contradictions.description: The initial state places W particles within a Cu matrix, whereas conformally coating each particle by ALD ordinarily requires precursor access to the entire particle surface before matrix embedding. The stated clean, accessible surfaces do not resolve how embedded particles remain fully accessible.
